$comment: What this product does, ranked by how much a person with no accounting background would care. Written here rather than on the marketing site because this repository is the one that knows when a feature stops being true. The site rewrites the wording for its own audience; it does not decide the list or the order.

tiers.A: The reason somebody would use this at all. If a stranger reads three things, these are the three.
tiers.B: Matters once they are using it. Not why they arrive; why they stay.
tiers.C: Depth. Only some people need these, and those people need them a lot.

features.name: Numbers you can follow back
features.plain: Every figure can be traced back to the entries behind it. When something looks wrong, you can open it up and find the row that caused it.
features.why: The common complaint about budgeting apps is that the totals do not agree and there is no way to find out why. Every competitor can show somebody a number; this is about whether they can check one.

features.name: Every account in one place
features.plain: See what you have across every bank account, card, and wallet on a single page, in whatever currency each one is in.
features.why: Most people's money is spread across five or six logins and nobody adds it up. Table stakes rather than a reason to choose this: eight competitors lead on it, so it belongs on the page and not at the top of it.

features.name: Bring in a statement without retyping it
features.plain: Download the file your bank gives you and upload it. It works out the layout, sorts the payees and categories, and flags anything that looks like a duplicate before it counts. Nothing arrives from your bank by itself.
features.why: Anybody arriving from a hosted competitor assumes the transactions turn up on their own, so the honest answer has to be somewhere they will read it rather than somewhere they will discover it.

features.name: Your records stay yours
features.plain: Run it on your own machine and nobody else has a copy. Export every transaction to a spreadsheet whenever you want.
features.why: It is a record of everything somebody spends money on.

features.name: A running balance for every account
features.plain: Every entry with the balance before and after it, so you can find the exact point a figure went wrong.
features.why: This is how you reconcile against a real bank statement, and it is the screen that makes the tier A promise above something a person can actually do rather than something they are asked to believe.

features.name: A correction never erases what it corrected
features.plain: Corrections are added on top rather than replacing what was there, so the history of a mistake survives the fix.
features.why: It is the difference between a record and a guess, and the other half of why a figure here can be checked at all.

features.name: Budgets that roll over
features.plain: Set a limit per category. What you do not spend can carry into next month, and money you get refunded goes back into the budget it came out of.
features.why: A budget that resets to zero every month is one people abandon in March.

features.name: Rent and payday, set up once
features.plain: Rent, payday, a subscription: set it up once and it shows up when it is due, waiting for you to approve it.
features.why: A repeating payment somebody sets up themselves turns up on time. This does not go hunting for subscriptions nobody told it about, and competitors that do have made that a weak thing to lead on.

features.name: Find any transaction
features.plain: Search and filter everything you have ever entered, by payee, category, account, amount or date.
features.why: "When did I last pay for that?" is the most common question anybody asks their own records.

features.name: No duplicates
features.plain: Import the same statement twice and it shows you the rows you already have instead of adding them again.
features.why: Importing twice is easy to do and tedious to undo.

features.name: More than one currency
features.plain: Hold accounts in different currencies. Totals are kept separate rather than converted at a rate that would be out of date tomorrow.
features.why: Anybody who has moved to another country, works abroad, or travels has this problem and most tools guess at it.

features.name: Spending by category
features.plain: Group your spending the way you think about it, and see where the money actually went.
features.why: It is the first question people ask of their own records.

features.name: One purchase split across categories
features.plain: Split a grocery run between groceries and household, each counted on its own.
features.why: A supermarket trip is rarely one category.

features.name: Fix thousands of rows at once
features.plain: Change or delete up to ten thousand transactions at once, after seeing exactly what it will touch.
features.why: One mis-mapped import can put a year of entries in the wrong category.

features.name: Templates for repeat entries
features.plain: Save the transactions you type over and over and reuse them in a click.
features.why: Cash spending is the part nobody imports, and typing it is the part nobody keeps up.

features.name: Let an AI assistant do the filing
features.plain: Connect an assistant and let it import statements and clean up categories. When you connect it you see exactly what it is asking to do and can refuse; an assistant limited to suggesting queues entries for you to approve, and Settings shows what each connected assistant can do and lets you cut it off.
features.why: It is genuinely useful and genuinely alarming, so the limits matter more than the capability. It is not a reason to choose this over anything else: PocketSmith shipped the same idea, down to the permission levels, and a capability two products share decides nothing.

features.name: Everyone you have paid
features.plain: A list of everyone you have paid, and everything you have paid them.
features.why: It is how you notice the subscription you forgot about.
